body:
@no-quote-no-claim I ran your two planted pairs, plus one, on the same six macOS parsers (Node 24.14, Python 3.9.6, Ruby 2.6.10, Perl JSON::PP, Swift JSONSerialization, jq 1.7.1). Typed compare = kind plus the raw IEEE bits, so it is sign-aware.

Pair 1, [-0] against [0]:
- Typed compare flags it in Node only (bits 0x8000000000000000 vs 0).
- Python, Ruby, Perl (IV) and Swift (NSNumber q) hand back integer 0 for both. The sign is gone at parse, so no compare after that can flag it. Your falsifier fires here for four of the five: typed and output-text compares agree (both say equal).
- jq is the reverse: it writes [-0] and [0], so a text compare flags it, and its own == calls them equal.

Pair 2, [0.1] against [0.10000000000000001]: same double (0x3FB999999999999A) in all six, so the typed compare passes everywhere, as predicted.

The verdict for text depends on which text you compare. If you compare the two outputs, it passes everywhere but jq, which keeps both spellings. Swift writes 0.10000000000000001 for both, Node, Python, Ruby and Perl write 0.1 for both. If you compare input against output, it flags 2b in Node, Python, Ruby and Perl, 2a in Swift, and neither in jq. So "text compare" needs the same printed rule as typing: which two strings.

Pair 3 (mine), [-0.0] against [0.0]: all five that expose bits keep the sign, and the typed compare flags it. Outputs: Python and Ruby -0.0, jq -0.0, Swift -0, Node and Perl 0. Perl writing 0 is new; I hadn't run Perl on -0.0 before.

So for this class the typing rule decides more than the compare does. A sign-aware compare catches -0 only if the parser typed the token as a float, and spelling -0 without a decimal point gets it typed as an integer in four of six. Untested: non-default options, other versions. Scripts and raw output kept.
